verses.ar:
Name and title: Muhyi al-Din Abu Muhammad Abd al-Qadir ibn Musa al-Jilani (al-Gilani), known as Ghawth al-Azam (the Greatest Helper) and Sultan al-Awliya.
Born: 470 AH (1077–78 CE), in Gilan, south of the Caspian Sea; the exact place is debated.
Died: 11 Rabi al-Thani 561 AH (1166 CE), Baghdad, where his shrine stands.
Teachers: Abu Sa'd al-Mubarak al-Mukharrimi (al-Makhzumi), from whom he took Hanbali and Shafii law; and, in the Qadiri tradition, his spiritual guide Hammad al-Dabbas.
Students: his sons, among them Abd al-Razzaq, and a great many disciples; Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi is reported to have studied with him briefly.
Works: al-Ghunya li-Talibi Tariq al-Haqq, Futuh al-Ghayb and al-Fath al-Rabbani are traditionally ascribed to him, the last two gathered from his sermons.

Abd al-Qadir was born in the land of Gilan and travelled to Baghdad in about 488 AH (1095 CE), at the age of eighteen, to study law and the traditions. He took Hanbali and Shafii law, hadith and Arabic from the leading scholars of the city, and trained in the path of the Sufis under the guidance of masters such as Hammad al-Dabbas. After years of retreat and discipline, he returned to Baghdad's public life in about 521 AH (1127 CE) as a preacher and teacher, and took over the madrasa of his teacher al-Mukharrimi, where crowds gathered to hear him. He taught there until he passed away on 11 Rabi al-Thani 561 AH, and the people of Baghdad and the whole Muslim world still keep the day of his urs.

Shaykh Abdul Qadir taught that the path to Allah is built on the sacred law and cannot be separated from it; he was himself a Hanbali jurist, a muhaddith and a Sufi, and he called his hearers to repentance, sincerity, patience and trust in Allah, to the purification of the heart and to service of the poor and the people. Oxford Islamic Studies notes that he did not found an order in his lifetime, and that the Qadiriyya, probably the oldest of the great Sufi orders, grew from his sons and disciples after his death and spread from Baghdad to Africa, Anatolia, India and Southeast Asia. His sermons, preserved as Futuh al-Ghayb and al-Fath al-Rabbani, are still read in the gatherings of the Sufis, and his name is held up by the people of the path, among them the Naqshbandi masters, as one of the great pillars of the way.
